meta.title: The non-commodity cost stack
meta.subtitle: Roughly a third of a household electricity bill is neither the energy nor the supplier's margin. It is delivery, and it is policy.
meta.one_line: Between the wholesale price a supplier pays and the unit rate a household is charged sit two large blocks that have nothing to do with buying electricity: the cost of moving it, and the cost of the policies attached to it. They are set by regulators and network companies rather than by markets, they are collected through the bill, and they have moved far more than the wholesale price does in an ordinary year.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every levy, obligation and network charge here is published — in HMRC rate tables, Ofgem decisions, DESNZ policy documents and network company statements — so the simulated company reads them exactly as a real supplier does. The simulation's own per-period attribution of these costs is a separate matter and is described in its own rung.

claim_freshness.source: HMRC CCL rate tables; Ofgem RO buy-out and mutualisation publications; LCCC CfD levy determinations; DESNZ Green Gas Levy rates; Ofgem cap methodology annexes; NAO 'Energy supplier failures' (Nov 2022).
claim_freshness.route: Assembled from this repository's own sourced research (docs/institutional/knowledge_map.md and docs/market_research/) and cross-checked against the rate tables the simulation actually settles against in simulation/policy_costs.py.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A household electricity bill is not mostly the electricity. Roughly a quarter of it pays for the wires that deliver it and roughly an eighth pays for policies attached to it — renewables support, capacity procurement, feed-in tariffs, and the socialised cost of other suppliers going bust — and because those are set administratively rather than cleared in a market, they can be **negative**, they can **step**, and they can arrive **retrospectively**.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Think of the unit rate as a stack rather than a price.

At the bottom is the **wholesale cost** — what your supplier actually paid for the energy. On top of that sits **network cost**: the charge for the transmission lines and the local distribution network that physically delivered it. Then **policy cost**: a set of levies the government has chosen to fund through electricity bills rather than through taxation. Then the supplier's own **operating cost** and whatever **margin** it makes. Then VAT.

The striking thing is how little of that stack the supplier controls. It can hedge the wholesale block. It cannot negotiate the network charge, and it cannot decline the levies — its only choices are how accurately it forecasts them and whether it passes them through.

And they do not behave like prices. A market price wanders. These **step**, on dates set by decisions: a levy is introduced, a rate is rebalanced, a network charging methodology changes and a cost that used to sit in your unit rate turns up in your standing charge instead. A supplier that models them as smooth will be wrong on exactly the days that matter.

The strangest case is the one that pays you back. In 2022, when wholesale prices went far above the fixed prices guaranteed to some renewable generators, the mechanism that normally collects money from suppliers to pay those generators ran **in reverse** and rebated them instead. A cost line went negative.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
**Network charges — the cost of delivery.** Two layers: transmission (the national high-voltage system) and distribution (the local network). Domestic and small-business supply pays both through a per-unit charge and a standing charge; larger industrial sites connected higher up the network face a different mix, and their transmission charge is driven by demand at the system's peak moments rather than by annual volume. A structural change in 2023 moved part of the transmission residual out of the per-unit charge and into a **banded fixed charge**, which changes who pays what without changing the total collected — a supplier that kept modelling it per-unit would misprice low-consumption customers in one direction and high-consumption ones in the other.

**The Renewables Obligation.** Suppliers must present a number of certificates per MWh supplied, or pay a **buy-out price** per certificate short. The obligation level and the buy-out price are both set annually, so the effective cost per MWh is the product of two administratively-set numbers and has risen substantially across the last decade.

**Contracts for Difference.** Generators hold contracts at a fixed **strike price**. When the market price is below the strike, suppliers fund the difference; when the market price is **above** it, the flow reverses and suppliers are paid. This is why the CfD line was a cost for most of the period, went to zero, and then turned **negative during the 2022 price crisis** — the mechanism did exactly what it was designed to do, and a model that assumed levies are non-negative got the crisis wrong in the direction of pessimism.

**Capacity Market and Feed-in Tariff levies** are collected from all segments including domestic, and fund capacity availability payments and legacy small-scale generation respectively.

**Climate Change Levy** is a tax on business energy use — domestic supply is exempt — with separate rates for electricity and gas. The gas rate was deliberately raised over several years to bring it toward parity with the electricity rate, which is a policy choice about which fuel to discourage, visible directly in the rate table.

**Mutualisation — the cost of other people's failures.** When a supplier fails, its unpaid obligations do not vanish: they are recovered from the surviving suppliers in proportion to volume. The 2021–22 failure wave made this a material per-MWh cost for two years and then largely receded. It is a levy in everything but name, and it is one no supplier can forecast from its own book.

**Gas has its own stack**, smaller and differently shaped: transportation charges across the national and regional networks, the Climate Change Levy for business users, and a per-meter Green Gas Levy introduced in late 2021 to fund biomethane injection.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
**Steps, not slopes.** Plotted per MWh over a decade, these lines should be visibly piecewise — flat stretches broken by discrete jumps on policy dates. A smooth curve is a sign the model has interpolated something that was decided, not discovered.

**At least one line below zero.** A cost stack in which every component is non-negative across 2016–2025 has failed to represent the CfD mechanism, and will overstate supplier costs precisely in the crisis year when the question mattered most.

**A two-year bump that is nobody's fault.** Mutualisation should appear as near-zero for the first half of the period, spike across the failure wave, and decay. If it is a constant, it is a fudge.

**Domestic and business should diverge on CCL and nowhere else.** Domestic supply is exempt from the Climate Change Levy and pays every other line. A model where segments differ everywhere is not applying the exemptions; one where they differ nowhere is not applying them either.

**The stack should be a large minority of the bill, not a rounding error.** If network plus policy is a couple of percent, something is being dropped — most likely the standing-charge half.

live_evidence.heading: What this simulation actually does
live_evidence.body:
These are not a single blended adder. Each is settled **per half-hourly period, per customer, with its own rate table**, and each lands on the settlement record as its own field — the Renewables Obligation, the CfD levy, the Capacity Market levy, the Feed-in Tariff levy, the Climate Change Levy, the mutualisation levy and network cost are seven separate numbers, not one. That is why the margin bridge can attribute a year's change to a levy rather than to "costs".

The rates are **year-indexed tables built from published sources**, not curve fits: `simulation/policy_costs.py` carries them with the derivation and the source named beside each block, and the market-research notes behind them are in `docs/market_research/`. The CfD levy goes negative in 2022 because the published determination did; the mutualisation levy is near-zero until the failure wave, peaks, and decays, because that is what happened.

Segment exemptions are applied rather than assumed: domestic supply pays no Climate Change Levy, business supply does, and the industrial and commercial network treatment differs from the domestic one.

On the company side these obligations are not only a cost line — they are a **statutory return**. The supplier assembles what it owes from its own supply volumes, which is the same direction of reasoning a real supplier's regulatory reporting takes.

residuals.heading: What this page does not settle
residuals.body:
**The network numbers are the least certain thing here, and the repository says so.** Our own research notes record that the per-year network figures used differ from the cap methodology's published annex by several pounds per MWh, and that the 2023 structural change moving part of the transmission residual into a banded standing charge is not fully modelled. That is a known, recorded discrepancy rather than a settled figure, and it is the most likely source of error in any per-customer cost-to-serve conclusion drawn from this simulation.

**Rates beyond the published horizon are extrapolated.** Some tables are extended past the last published year. Every figure after that point is an assumption wearing a number, and the further out it goes the more it is worth distrusting.

**Mutualisation is annualised industry cost divided by industry volume.** That is a reasonable proxy and it is not how any individual supplier was actually billed — the real recovery is lumpy, follows specific events, and lands on specific dates.

**The Green Gas Levy is per meter per day and is normalised here to a per-MWh figure.** That conversion depends on assumed annual consumption, so it is exactly right in aggregate and wrong for any individual meter whose consumption is atypical.

scope_delta.heading: Where the simulation stops
scope_delta.body: No obligation trading: a real supplier can buy and sell Renewables Obligation certificates, manage its position across the compliance year and choose the buy-out route deliberately. Here the cost is accrued per unit supplied and settled. No Triad avoidance behaviour beyond exposure measurement — large sites really do reshape demand to dodge peak transmission charges, and that is a commercial strategy this company does not run. No forecasting error on the levies themselves: the simulation applies the rate that was actually set, where a real supplier prices a fixed-term contract against a levy rate that has not been announced yet, and carries the risk of guessing wrong. And no CCL relief schemes — the reliefs available to energy-intensive industry through climate change agreements are named nowhere in this model.
